strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: learning from feedback naturally expressed during user–LLM conversations. It presents a concrete pipeline producing 20,281 preference examples, with both GPT-4-generated and policy-generated response variants.

The GPT-4-data results provide meaningful evidence of practical utility across three model families. For example, Phi 3 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on length-controlled AlpacaEval and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. Length-controlled results help establish that the gains are not solely due to verbosity.

The feedback detector receives a human audit involving four annotators and 50 conversations. Its agreement with adjudicated labels approaches the reported human–human agreement, providing useful validation of this pipeline stage.

The manuscript supplies detailed annotation and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters. The reported separation of test users and conversations from training is also a valuable safeguard.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. Comparisons are against off-the-shelf models, without a matched control using GPT-4 responses generated on the same prompts without feedback, an SFT-only ablation, or training on an existing preference dataset. Consequently, improvements could substantially reflect teacher distillation and additional training. The expert/on-policy comparison also changes response sources, dataset sizes, and filtering, limiting causal interpretation.

The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o summarizes preferences, generates expert responses, and judges responses against those summaries. Figure 2 demonstrates sensitivity to the supplied checklist, but does not establish that the checklist accurately represents users or that checklist-guided rankings agree better with human judgments. The human study evaluates SAT/DSAT classification only. A blinded audit of preference summaries and response rankings against the original feedback is needed.

The evaluation supports a narrower population claim than the manuscript makes. Section 4 deliberately selects preferences resembling others within task clusters and emphasizes similarity to training tasks. This does not establish representation of majority preferences or generalization across diverse users. Selection from feedback-bearing conversations introduces further coverage limitations, acknowledged in Section 6; DSAT recall is only 48.4% in the audit. A randomly sampled held-out evaluation and coverage analysis would better substantiate the broader claims.

The claim that either dataset version preserves performance on other benchmarks is contradicted by Table 3. On-policy Mistral falls from 17.1% to 12.9% on length-controlled AlpacaEval, 12.6% to 10.3% on Arena-Hard, and 6.71 to 6.42 on MT-Bench. These regressions need discussion. Confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates are also absent, limiting interpretation of smaller improvements described as significant.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied prompts and training settings. The dataset is only promised for future release, and the manuscript does not sufficiently specify generation settings, the preference-filtering procedure, clustering representations, or hyperparameter-selection criteria. These omissions affect reconstruction of both the training data and the custom benchmark. Together with the missing controls and independent preference validation, they warrant revision next cycle before a sound Findings recommendation.
